claim: Listening to speech evokes neural responses in the motor cortex in humans.
source: In humans, listening to speech evokes neural responses in the motor cortex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon that motivates the study.

claim: Motor cortex neural patterns during listening were substantially different than during articulation of the same sounds.
source: Motor cortex neural patterns during listening were substantially different than during articulation of the same sounds.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: During listening, neural activity was observed in the superior and inferior regions of ventral motor cortex.
source: During listening, we observed neural activity in the superior and inferior regions of ventral motor cortex.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: During speaking, responses were distributed throughout somatotopic representations of speech articulators in motor cortex.
source: During speaking, responses were distributed throughout somatotopic representations of speech articulators in motor cortex.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data comparing speaking and listening conditions.

claim: The structure of responses in motor cortex during listening was organized along acoustic features similar to auditory cortex, rather than along articulatory features as during speaking.
source: The structure of responses in motor cortex during listening was organized along acoustic features similar to auditory cortex, rather than along articulatory features as during speaking.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on MDS and clustering analyses of neural responses.

claim: Motor cortex does not contain articulatory representations of perceived actions in speech.
source: Motor cortex does not contain articulatory representations of perceived actions in speech, but rather, represents auditory vocal information.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the experimental findings.

claim: Motor cortex represents auditory vocal information during speech perception.
source: Motor cortex does not contain articulatory representations of perceived actions in speech, but rather, represents auditory vocal information.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the experimental findings.

claim: Sensory and motor cortices are engaged during perception.
source: For example, a number of studies have demonstrated that both sensory and motor cortices are engaged during perception (Gallese et al., 1996; Wilson et al., 2004; Tkach et al., 2007; Cogan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Listening to speech sounds evokes robust neural activity in the motor cortex in humans.
source: In humans, this phenomenon has been observed in the context of speech, where listening to speech sounds evokes robust neural activity in the motor cortex (Wilson et al., 2004; Pulvermüller et al., 2006; Edwards et al., 2010; Cogan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The motor theory of speech perception posits that the objects of speech perception are the intended phonetic gestures of the speaker.
source: One interpretation of the observed motor activity during speech perception is that "the objects of speech perception are the intended phonetic gestures of the speaker"- as posited by Liberman's motor theory of speech perception (Liberman et al., 1967; Liberman and Mattingly, 1985).
evidence: This is a description of an existing theory with citations.

claim: High gamma (70–150 Hz) cortical surface local field potentials strongly correlate with extracellular multi-unit neuronal spiking.
source: We focused our analysis on high gamma (70–150 Hz) cortical surface local field potentials, which strongly correlate with extracellular multi-unit neuronal spiking (Steinschneider et al., 2008; Ray and Maunsell, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: During listening, evoked responses spanned middle and posterior STG, with weaker responses in middle temporal gyrus (MTG).
source: During listening, evoked responses spanned middle and posterior STG as expected, with weaker responses in middle temporal gyrus (MTG) (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: In the vSMC, electrodes in the superior-most and inferior-most aspects demonstrated reliable and robust single-trial responses to speech sounds during passive listening.
source: In the vSMC, (composed of the pre- and post- central gyri) we found electrodes in the superior-most and inferior-most aspects (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, 2) that demonstrated reliable and robust single-trial responses to speech sounds during passive listening (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: 3 out of 5 subjects showed significant clustering of regions responsive to auditory stimuli.
source: By performing spatial clustering analysis on the electrode positions in each subject, we found that 3/5 subjects showed significant clustering of regions responsive to auditory stimuli (Hartigan's Dip statistic, p<0.05 (see Materials and methods); Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: When participants spoke CV syllables, articulatory movement-related cortical activity was well distributed throughout vSMC.
source: When participants spoke the same CV syllables, in contrast, articulatory movement-related cortical activity was well distributed throughout vSMC (Figure 1c), with auditory feedback cortical activity seen in the STG.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: 115 electrodes demonstrated significant neural activity in vSMC during listening across all participants.
source: Across all participants, we identified 115 electrodes that demonstrated significant neural activity in vSMC during listening (p<0.01, t-test, compared to pre-stimulus silent rest period; Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: 362 electrodes in vSMC were found to be significantly active during speaking.
source: When speaking, in contrast, a total of 362 electrodes in vSMC were found to be significantly active (Figure 1d, p<0.01, t-test, compared to pre-stimulus silent rest period).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Only approximately 27% of vSMC sites (98 out of 362) were active during both listening and speaking.
source: Critically, only a subset of sites in vSMC (98 out of 362, ~27%) was active during both listening and speaking (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Sites active during both listening and speaking were primarily localized to the pre-central gyrus.
source: These sites were primarily localized to the pre-central gyrus, whereas speaking evoked activity across both pre- and post-central gyri sites.
evidence: This is an observation from the spatial distribution of active electrodes.

claim: Neural responses in the vSMC during listening were found in the superior pre-central gyrus and inferior, anterior aspect of the sub-central gyrus of the vSMC.
source: Neural responses in the vSMC during listening were found in the superior (S in Figure 1d) pre-central gyrus and inferior, anterior aspect of the sub-central gyrus of the vSMC (I in Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a description of the spatial distribution of neural responses from the experimental data.

claim: The plosive consonants /b/, /d/, and /g/ are produced by the closure of the vocal tract at the lips, front tongue, and back tongue, respectively.
source: For example, the plosive consonants /b/, /d/, and /g/ are produced by the closure of the vocal tract at the lips, front tongue, and back tongue, respectively (Figure 2a, b, see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for all syllable tokens) (Ladefoged and Johnson, 2010).
evidence: This is established phonetic knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The cortical representations for speech articulators are laid out along a superior-to-inferior (medial-to-lateral) sequence in the vSMC.
source: The cortical representations for these articulators are laid out along a superior-to-inferior (medial-to-lateral) sequence in the vSMC (Penfield and Boldrey, 1937).
evidence: This is established neuroscientific knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The production of labial consonants (/b/) is associated with activity in lip cortical representations located superior to the tongue representations.
source: The production of labial consonants (/b/) is associated with activity in lip cortical representations as evidenced by strong responses to the bilabial /ba/ (Figure 2c, electrodes 5–6, blue lines). These are located superior to the tongue representations associated with the /d/ and /g/ consonants, as shown previously (Bouchard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data with reference to previous work.

claim: During listening, the majority of vSMC electrodes were not active.
source: We next examined those same vSMC electrodes during listening, and found that the majority of those cortical vSMC electrodes were not active (p>0.01, t-test compared to silence, Figure 2c transparent red lines).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The few vSMC electrodes that were active during listening were similar for all three CV syllables, with activity increasing approximately 100ms after the acoustic onset.
source: The few that were active (electrodes 1, 2, 4, 11–12, solid red lines) were similar for all three CV syllables, with activity increasing approximately 100ms after the acoustic onset.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data.

claim: Onset latencies in vSMC during listening were generally shorter than those in STG sites.
source: Across the entire population of vSMC electrodes that were active during listening, onset latencies were generally shorter than those in STG sites, with significant increases in both inferior vSMC (p<0.001) and superior vSMC (p<0.05) compared to STG (Figure 3a, Wilcoxon rank sum test, see Figure 3c for average responses to all syllables).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The latency to the response peak was significantly higher in superior vSMC compared to STG.
source: The latency to the response peak was also significantly higher in superior vSMC compared to STG (Figure 3b, p<0.01, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is a result from statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Cross-correlation analysis between vSMC and STG electrodes revealed a diverse array of relationships, including STG electrode activity leading vSMC electrode activity and vice versa.
source: A cross-correlation analysis between these vSMC electrodes and STG electrodes revealed a diverse array of relationships between these populations (Figure 3d–f), including STG electrode activity leading vSMC electrode activity and vice versa.
evidence: This is a result from cross-correlation analysis of the experimental data.

claim: During listening, the pattern of raw evoked responses shows critical differences from those during speaking.
source: In contrast to speaking, we did not observe somatotopic organization of cortical responses when listening to speech. Therefore, the pattern of raw evoked responses during listening shows critical differences from those during speaking.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: During speaking, evoked activity in vSMC clustered into place of articulation features: labials, alveolars, and velars.
source: Visual inspection of MDS plots shows that, during speaking, evoked activity in vSMC clustered into place of articulation features (Figure 4a): labials (/b/, /p/), alveolars (/s/, /sh/, /t/, /d/), and velars (/g/, /k/) (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a result from MDS analysis of the experimental data.

claim: During listening, neural responses in vSMC did not cluster into place of articulation features.
source: In contrast, neural responses during listening did not cluster into the same features (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a result from MDS analysis of the experimental data.

claim: While evoked activity during speaking clustered by place of articulation features, activity during listening did not.
source: We found that while evoked activity during speaking clustered by place of articulation features, activity during listening did not (Figure 4d; see Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for moving time window analysis).
evidence: This is a result from K-means clustering and adjusted Rand Index analysis.

claim: Even when the vSMC electrode subset was restricted to short-latency vSMC electrodes leading STG activity, activity during listening did not cluster according to place of articulation features.
source: Even when the vSMC electrode subset was restricted to short-latency vSMC electrodes leading STG activity (as evidenced by a positive asymmetry index in Figure 3f), activity during listening did not cluster according to place of articulation features (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from additional analysis to test whether early responses show articulatory organization.

claim: Responses in motor areas during speech perception do not show a spatially distributed representation of speech motor articulator features.
source: Thus, responses in motor areas during speech perception do not show a spatially distributed representation of speech motor articulator features.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the clustering analysis results.

claim: STG spatial patterns during listening showed clustering according to three high-order acoustic features: voiced plosives, unvoiced plosives, and fricatives.
source: Using multidimensional scaling, STG spatial patterns during listening showed clustering according to three high-order acoustic features (Figure 4e): voiced plosives (/b/, /d/, /g/), unvoiced plosives (/p/, /t/, /k/), and fricatives (/s/, /sh/) (Ladefoged and Johnson, 2010).
evidence: This is a result from MDS analysis of STG responses.

claim: Activity in motor cortex during listening clustered into the same three acoustic features as STG.
source: With the same analyses, we observed that activity in motor cortex clustered into the same three acoustic features (Figure 4f, note this panel is identical to Figure 4c simply re-colored).
evidence: This is a result from MDS analysis of vSMC responses during listening.

claim: vSMC activity during listening organized into linguistically defined acoustic feature groups, but was significantly weaker than the organization of STG.
source: Unsupervised K-means clustering analysis confirmed that vSMC activity, during listening, organized into these linguistically defined acoustic feature groups, but was significantly weaker than the organization of STG (p<0.001, Wilcoxon rank-sum, Figure 4g).
evidence: This is a result from K-means clustering and statistical comparison.

claim: Clustering by acoustic manner features was significantly stronger than clustering by place features in vSMC electrodes during listening.
source: Importantly, however, clustering by acoustic manner features was significantly stronger than clustering by place features in vSMC electrodes during listening (p<0.001, Wilcoxon rank-sum, Figure 4h).
evidence: This is a result from statistical comparison of clustering indices.

claim: Motor cortex activity during speech perception reflects an acoustic sensory representation of speech in the vSMC that mirrors acoustic representations of speech in auditory cortex.
source: This organization suggests that motor cortex activity during speech perception reflects an acoustic sensory representation of speech in the vSMC that mirrors acoustic representations of speech in auditory cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the clustering analysis results.

claim: 16 out of 98 vSMC sites were reasonably well-predicted with a linear STRF (r>=0.10 and p<0.01).
source: A fraction of vSMC sites (16/98 sites total) were reasonably well-predicted with a linear STRF (r>=0.10 and p<0.01, permutation test) (Theunissen et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from STRF modeling analysis.

claim: STRFs with significant correlation coefficients were localized to superior and inferior vSMC (primarily precentral gyrus) in addition to STG.
source: STRFs with significant correlation coefficients were localized to superior and inferior vSMC (primarily precentral gyrus) in addition to STG (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is a result from STRF analysis showing spatial distribution.

claim: The prediction performance of STRFs in vSMC was generally lower than that of the STG.
source: Still, the prediction performance of STRFs in vSMC was generally lower than that of the STG (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a result from comparing STRF prediction performance across regions.

claim: The majority of STRFs in both vSMC and STG showed strong low frequency tuning (100–200 Hz) properties related to voicing.
source: Furthermore, the majority of STRFs in both regions showed strong low frequency tuning (100–200 Hz) properties related to voicing (Figure 5c), though some also showed high frequency tuning consistent with selectivity for fricatives and stop consonants by visual inspection (Mesgarani et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a result from STRF analysis showing frequency tuning properties.

claim: Individual sites in motor cortex reflect sensory responses to definable spectrotemporal features of speech acoustics, including voicing attributes.
source: These findings reveal that individual sites in motor cortex reflect sensory responses to definable spectrotemporal features speech acoustics, including voicing attributes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the STRF analysis results.

claim: The tuning properties of individual vSMC sites give rise to the acoustic organization found in the distributed spatial patterns of neural activity.
source: Presumably, this tuning gives rise to the acoustic organization found in the previous analysis of distributed spatial patterns of neural activity.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the STRF results to the clustering results.

claim: Mirror neurons in area F5 of macaques fire both when a monkey produced an action and observed a similar action.
source: The proposal that the motor cortex critically integrates observations with motor commands largely stems from the discovery of mirror neurons (in area F5 of macaques) that fire both when a monkey produced an action and observed a similar action (di Pellegrino et al., 1992; Rizzolatti and Craighero, 2004; Pulvermüller and Fadiga, 2010).
evidence: This is established neuroscientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Human neuroimaging studies have showed mirror activity in ventral premotor cortex during listening.
source: In line with these theories, human neuroimaging studies have showed mirror activity in ventral premotor cortex during listening (Wilson et al., 2004; Pulvermüller et al., 2006; Edwards et al., 2010), and modulated premotor activity in phoneme categorization tasks (Alho et al., 2012; Chevillet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research supported by citations.

claim: The study demonstrated local 'audiomotor' responses to speech sounds in vSMC.
source: Consistent with previous findings, we demonstrated local 'audiomotor' responses to speech sounds in vSMC.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Major motor articulatory place features (labial, alveolar, and velar) were not represented with single site activity or distributed spatial activity in vSMC during listening.
source: When the responses were further examined for phonetic structure, we found major motor articulatory place features, such as labial, alveolar, and velar, were not represented with single site activity or distributed spatial activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings from the clustering analysis.

claim: The observation that place features are not represented in vSMC during listening is in direct contrast with structural predictions made by the original motor theory of speech perception.
source: This observation is in direct contrast with structural predictions made by the original motor theory of speech perception (Liberman et al., 1967; Liberman and Mattingly, 1985), while confirming that motor cortex plays a role in perception (Lindblom, 1996; Hickok and Poeppel, 2007).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in relation to existing theories.

claim: Activity during speech perception was localized to regions of the vSMC that have been implicated in phonation and laryngeal control.
source: We localized activity during speech perception to regions of the vSMC that have been implicated in phonation and laryngeal control (Penfield and Boldrey, 1937; Brown et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding from the study with reference to previous anatomical knowledge.

claim: When listening to speech, regions of vSMC implicated in phonation and laryngeal control reflected acoustic sensory properties of speech, with individual sites tuned for spectrotemporal acoustic properties.
source: When listening to speech, we observed these regions reflected acoustic sensory properties of speech, with individual sites tuned for spectrotemporal acoustic properties.
evidence: This is a summary of the STRF analysis findings.

claim: The tuning properties of responsive sites in vSMC are similar to properties observed in STG during listening.
source: The tuning properties of responsive sites in vSMC are similar to properties observed in STG during listening (Mesgarani et al., 2014) and appear to give rise to an acoustic sensory organization of speech sounds (rather than purely motor organization) in motor cortex during listening.
evidence: This is a comparison of findings with previous research.

claim: Frontal and motor regions are recruited during effortful listening.
source: There is an emerging consensus that frontal and motor regions are recruited during effortful listening (Du et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a summary of emerging consensus in the field with a citation.

claim: Frontal areas come online to process degraded speech for the attentional enhancement of auditory processing.
source: For example, previous studies have demonstrated that frontal areas come online to process degraded speech for the attentional enhancement of auditory processing (Wild et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a summary of previous research with a citation.

claim: The audiomotor cortex enhancement is specific to an auditory representation, without transforming information to a motor articulatory representation.
source: Our results may complement this interpretation in that the audiomotor cortex enhancement is specific to an auditory representation, without transforming information to a motor articulatory representation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings in relation to previous work.

claim: The auditory encoding observed in the motor cortex did not appear to be as strong as that observed in the STG.
source: That being said, the auditory encoding that we observed in the motor cortex did not appear to be as strong as that as that observed in the STG, and exhibited comparatively weaker activity and weaker phoneme selectivity (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b and c, and see (Mesgarani et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison of findings between vSMC and STG.

claim: Auditory feedback is potentially processed directly in the vSMC in addition to the canonical auditory cortex.
source: In addition to having implications for perceptual models, we speculate that these results have strong implications for speech production, as auditory feedback is potentially processed directly in the vSMC in addition to the canonical auditory cortex.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Speech production models propose pathways for the activation of auditory cortex from vSMC activation (forward prediction) and the activation of vSMC from auditory and somatosensory input (error correction signal).
source: Speech production models currently propose a complex role for sensory feedback, where pathways exist for the activation of auditory cortex from vSMC activation (the forward prediction of production consequences), and the activation of vSMC from auditory and somatosensory input (the error correction signal) (Guenther et al., 2006; Houde and Nagarajan, 2011).
evidence: This is a summary of existing speech production models with citations.

claim: The motor cortex contains both sensory and motor representations, where the sensory representations are active during passive listening, whereas motor representations dominate during speech production.
source: In the current study, it appears that the motor cortex contains both sensory and motor representations, where the sensory representations are active during passive listening, whereas motor representations dominate during speech production.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Early responses in vSMC may reflect bidirectional connections from STG, primary auditory cortex, or auditory thalamus.
source: Early responses in vSMC may reflect bidirectional connections from STG (Zatorre et al., 2007), primary auditory cortex (Nelson et al., 2013; Schneider et al., 2014) or auditory thalamus (Henschke et al., 2014), whereas later responses might reflect indirect connectivity in areas downstream from the STG (Rauschecker and Scott, 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the latency findings with citations to anatomical connectivity studies.

claim: Later responses in vSMC might reflect indirect connectivity in areas downstream from the STG.
source: Early responses in vSMC may reflect bidirectional connections from STG (Zatorre et al., 2007), primary auditory cortex (Nelson et al., 2013; Schneider et al., 2014) or auditory thalamus (Henschke et al., 2014), whereas later responses might reflect indirect connectivity in areas downstream from the STG (Rauschecker and Scott, 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the latency findings with a citation.

claim: Activity in vSMC from speech sounds may be a consequence of sounds activating the sensory feedback circuit.
source: Given these proposed functional connections, activity in vSMC from speech sounds may be a consequence of sounds activating the sensory feedback circuit (Hickok et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings with a citation.

claim: Evoked responses in the motor cortex during passive listening directly reflecting auditory inputs arising from aggregated activity picked up by the electrode is less likely given that auditory responses were observed in dorsal vSMC on electrode contacts several centimeters away from auditory inputs in the STG.
source: Alternatively, evoked responses in the motor cortex during passive listening may directly reflect auditory inputs arising from aggregated activity picked up by the electrode. We believe the latter scenario to be less likely, however, given that auditory responses were observed in dorsal vSMC on electrode contacts several centimeters away from auditory inputs in the STG.
evidence: This is an argument against an alternative interpretation based on spatial considerations.

claim: The spatial spread of neural signals in the high gamma range is substantially smaller than the distance between vSMC and STG electrodes.
source: In addition, the spatial spread of neural signals in the high gamma range is substantially smaller than this difference – high gamma signal correlations at <2 mm spacing are only around r=0.5, and at distances of 1 cm reach a noise floor (Chang, 2015); Muller et al, unpublished findings).
evidence: This is a technical argument based on signal properties with citations.

claim: Motor theories of speech perception may need to be revised to incorporate a novel sensorimotor representation of sound in the vSMC.
source: Given the observed acoustic rather than place selectivity observed during listening in the vSMC, our results suggest that motor theories of speech perception may need to be revised to incorporate a novel sensorimotor representation of sound in the vSMC.
evidence: This is a conclusion and recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: Nine human participants were implanted with high-density multi-electrode cortical surface arrays as part of their clinical evaluation for epilepsy surgery.
source: Nine human participants were implanted with high-density multi-electrode cortical surface arrays as part of their clinical evaluation for epilepsy surgery.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: The electrode array contained 256 electrodes with 4 mm pitch.
source: The array contained 256 electrodes with 4 mm pitch.
evidence: This is a description of the recording equipment.

claim: All participants were left hemisphere language dominant, as assessed by the Wada test.
source: All participants were left hemisphere language dominant, as assessed by the Wada test.
evidence: This is a description of participant characteristics.

claim: Participants had self-reported normal hearing.
source: Participants had self-reported normal hearing.
evidence: This is a description of participant characteristics.

claim: Participants listened to eight consonant-vowel (CV) syllables produced by a male speaker unknown to the participant.
source: First, participants listened to eight consonant-vowel (CV) syllables (/ba/, /da/, /ga/, /pa/, /ta/, /ka/, /∫a/, /sa/) produced by a male speaker unknown to the participant.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental task.

claim: Stimuli were presented randomly, with 4–21 repetitions of each CV syllable for 5 out of the 9 subjects, and one repetition of each CV syllable for 4 subjects.
source: Stimuli were presented randomly, with 4–21 repetitions of each CV syllable for 5 out of the 9 subjects included in all subsequent analyses, and one repetition of each CV syllable for 4 subjects shown only in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Participants spoke aloud the same CV syllables prompted by a visual cue on the laptop computer display.
source: In the second task, participants spoke aloud the same CV syllables prompted by a visual cue on the laptop computer display.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental task.

claim: Participants passively listened to natural speech samples from a phonemically transcribed continuous speech corpus (TIMIT).
source: In the third task, participants passively listened to natural speech samples from a phonemically transcribed continuous speech corpus (TIMIT).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental task.

claim: 499 unique sentences from 400 different male and female speakers were chosen from TIMIT, with each sentence repeated two times.
source: We chose 499 unique sentences from 400 different male and female speakers. Each sentence was repeated two times.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: Electrocorticographic (ECoG) signals were recorded with a multichannel PZ2 amplifier connected to an RZ2 digital signal acquisition system sampling at 3,052 Hz.
source: Electrocorticographic (ECoG) signals were recorded with a multichannel PZ2 amplifier connected to an RZ2 digital signal acquisition system (Tucker-Davis Technologies, Alachua, FL, USA) sampling at 3,052 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the data acquisition methods.

claim: The adjusted Rand Index (RIadj) quantifies the degree of agreement between two clustering patterns, where RIadj = 1 denotes identical clustering patterns and RIadj = 0 denotes independent clustering patterns.
source: The RIadj quantifies the degree of agreement between two clustering patterns, where RIadj = 1 denotes identical clustering patterns and RIadj = 0 denotes independent clustering patterns.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical method used.

claim: STG onset latencies were significantly lower than both inferior vSMC (p<0.001) and superior vSMC (p<0.05).
source: STG onset latencies were significantly lower than both inferior vSMC (p<0.001, Z = −4.03) and superior vSMC (p<0.05, Z = −2.28).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the latency analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: STG peak latencies were significantly lower than superior vSMC (p<0.01), but not significantly different from peak latencies in inferior vSMC.
source: STG peak latencies were significantly lower than superior vSMC (p<0.01, Z = −2.93), but not significantly different from peak latencies in inferior vSMC (p>0.1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the latency analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Cortical processing of speech sounds is spatially discrete and temporally fast.
source: Since cortical processing of speech sounds is spatially discrete and temporally fast (Formisano et al., 2008; Chang et al., 2011; Steinschneider et al., 2011), we used customized high-density electrode grids (a four-fold increase over conventional recordings) (Bouchard et al., 2013; Mesgarani et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge about speech processing supported by citations, used to justify the methodology.

claim: High-density electrode grids provide a four-fold increase over conventional recordings.
source: Since cortical processing of speech sounds is spatially discrete and temporally fast (Formisano et al., 2008; Chang et al., 2011; Steinschneider et al., 2011), we used customized high-density electrode grids (a four-fold increase over conventional recordings) (Bouchard et al., 2013; Mesgarani et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the recording technology used in the study.

claim: The vSMC is composed of the pre- and post-central gyri.
source: In the vSMC, (composed of the pre- and post- central gyri) we found electrodes in the superior-most and inferior-most aspects (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, 2) that demonstrated reliable and robust single-trial responses to speech sounds during passive listening (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is an anatomical definition provided in the manuscript.

claim: Two subjects showed k=2 electrode clusters (subjects 1 and 4, clusters in inferior and superior vSMC), and one subject showed k=5 clusters.
source: Out of these 3 subjects, k-means clustering revealed two subjects with k=2 electrode clusters (subjects 1 and 4, clusters in inferior and superior vSMC), and one subject with k=5 clusters.
evidence: This is a result from the spatial clustering analysis.
